stats.line: About 1 in 7 Americans aged 18 to 25 met the doctors' checklist for a drinking problem in the past year.
stats.mirror: You're under 26, drink most weekends, and wonder if it's a problem.

basis.design: national household survey (NSDUH), figures published by NIAAA
basis.who: people aged 18 to 25
basis.n: The survey interviews about 70,000 people aged 12 and up each year; NIAAA doesn't say how many were aged 18 to 25
basis.measured: Survey answers scored against the 11 signs of alcohol use disorder (DSM-5). Two or more signs in the past year counts, from mild to severe. College students 14.5%, others 15.3%.

stats.caveat: Mild cases count: 2 of 11 signs is enough. It is what people said in a survey, not a doctor's exam.

ref.cite: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (2025). Alcohol and Young Adults Ages 18 to 25 (2024 NSDUH data). NIAAA.
ref.quote: According to the 2024 NSDUH, 14.4% of adults ages 18 to 25 met the criteria for past-year alcohol use disorder (AUD).

stats.line: 9 in 10 Americans who drink too much, mostly by binging, aren't dependent. Even binging 10+ times a month, over two-thirds aren't.
stats.mirror: You drink hard on weekends and are sure you're not an alcoholic.

basis.design: national household survey (NSDUH), pooled 3 years
basis.who: adults 18+ who drank in the past year
basis.n: About 54,100 'excessive drinkers' (of 138,100 adults surveyed)
basis.measured: Share of 'excessive drinkers' who met DSM-IV dependence (3 of 7 signs in a year). Excessive = binge, heavy (15+ drinks a week for men), any drinking under 21, or while pregnant. Dependence was 4.3% at 1–2 binges a month, 29.8% at 10+.

stats.caveat: Not dependent is not the same as no harm. 'Dependent' here is the older, stricter label: 3 of 7 signs in one year.

ref.cite: Esser MB, Hedden SL, Kanny D, Brewer RD, Gfroerer JC, Naimi TS (2014). Prevalence of alcohol dependence among US adult drinkers, 2009-2011. Preventing Chronic Disease.
ref.quote: Most excessive drinkers (90%) did not meet the criteria for alcohol dependence.

stats.line: About 1 in 4 American men had 5 or more drinks in one sitting at least once in the past month.
stats.mirror: You have five or more drinks on a big night out.

basis.design: national household survey (NSDUH), figures published by NIAAA
basis.who: men aged 18 and older
basis.n: The survey interviews about 70,000 people aged 12 and up each year; NIAAA doesn't say how many were men
basis.measured: Binge drinking: 5 or more drinks on the same occasion (4 for women) on at least one day in the past 30 days. NIAAA's young-adults page gives 26.7% for ages 18 to 25.

stats.caveat: One such night in a month is enough to count. It says nothing about how often, or whether it is a problem.

ref.cite: National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (2025). Alcohol Use in the United States: Age Groups and Demographic Characteristics (2024 NSDUH data). NIAAA.
ref.quote: reported binge drinking in the past month … 31.8 million men ages 18 and older (24.9% in this age group)

stats.line: Of Americans who ever got hooked on alcohol, almost half were hooked before 21, and two in three before 25.
stats.mirror: You've been drinking since school and think it's just a phase.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews
basis.who: adults who had ever been dependent on alcohol
basis.n: 4,778 adults who had ever been hooked (of 43,093 surveyed)
basis.measured: The age at which each person first met the DSM-IV signs of alcohol dependence, as they recalled it. 15% before 18, 47% before 21.

stats.caveat: This counts only people who did get hooked. It does not mean most young drinkers get hooked; most don't.

ref.cite: Hingson RW, Heeren T, Winter MR (2006). Age of alcohol-dependence onset: associations with severity of dependence and seeking treatment. Pediatrics.
ref.quote: Of persons ever alcohol dependent, 15% were diagnosable before age 18, 47% before age 21, and two thirds before age 25.

stats.line: Nearly 1 in 4 people who drink are projected to get hooked at some point in life. For half of those, it took about 13 years from the first drink.
stats.mirror: You drank for years without trouble, but skipping a night feels harder now.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC, two waves), survival analysis
basis.who: adults who had ever had a full drink of alcohol
basis.n: 28,907 adults who had ever drunk alcohol; 4,822 of them became dependent
basis.measured: Age at first drink and age at first meeting DSM-IV dependence (3 of 7 signs in a year). Only about 2.0% were hooked within a year of starting, 11.0% within 10 years.

stats.caveat: A projection from what people recalled, not a count of people followed for life. For cigarettes the figure is 67.5%.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Pérez de los Cobos J, Hasin DS, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of transition from first use to dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis, and cocaine: results of the NESARC. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: 22.7% for alcohol users … Half of the cases of dependence on nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine were observed approximately 27, 13, 5 and 4 years after use onset

stats.line: After a heavy drinking night (7 drinks on average), the body's recovery score in the first 3 hours of sleep dropped about 39 points. After a light night: about 9.
stats.mirror: You sleep eight hours after drinking and still wake up wrecked.

basis.design: real-world study; each person compared with himself on nights with and without alcohol
basis.who: Finnish employees, mean age 45, 56% women
basis.n: 716 people on heavy nights (of 4,098 in the study)
basis.when: Published 2018; the paper doesn't give the years of the recordings
basis.measured: A heart-rate-based 'recovery' score over the first 3 hours of sleep. Low = up to 0.25 g alcohol per kg body weight; high = over 0.75 g/kg (one portion = 12 g).

stats.caveat: A heart signal of rest from a chest strap, not a full sleep study. Two authors worked for the company that makes the strap.

ref.cite: Pietilä J, Helander E, Korhonen I, Myllymäki T, Kujala UM, Lindholm H (2018). Acute effect of alcohol intake on cardiovascular autonomic regulation during the first hours of sleep in a large real-world sample of Finnish employees. JMIR Mental Health.
ref.quote: HRV-derived physiological recovery state decreased on average by 9.3, 24.0, and 39.2 percentage units with low, moderate, and high alcohol intake, respectively.

stats.line: In England, people who drink at risky levels spend about £18.60 a week on alcohol, on average. That is every single week.
stats.mirror: You've never added up the bar tabs and the bottles at home.

basis.design: monthly national survey (new sample each month)
basis.who: adults 18+ who drink at risky levels (5 or more on the AUDIT-C quiz)
basis.n: 44,382 risky drinkers surveyed 2014–2023; £18.60 is the October 2023 figure
basis.measured: Self-reported average weekly spend on alcohol, adjusted for inflation. £18.60 is the October 2023 figure.

stats.caveat: An average over everyone scoring 5+ on a short quiz, many of them lighter drinkers. Your own spend may be far higher or lower.

ref.cite: Jackson S, Oldham M, Angus C, Garnett C, Wilson L, Holmes J, Brown J (2024). Trends in alcohol expenditure among risky drinkers: a population study in England, 2014-2023. International Journal of Drug Policy.
ref.quote: There was an uncertain decrease in mean weekly expenditure from £18.90 … and subsequent rise to £18.60 [£17.90-£19.40] by October-2023.

stats.line: Of Americans once hooked on alcohol, only 1 in 4 were still hooked in the past year. And only 1 in 4 had ever had treatment.
stats.mirror: You want to quit drinking but won't go to rehab or AA.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews
basis.who: adults whose alcohol dependence began before the past year
basis.n: 4,422 adults who had been hooked before the past year (of 43,093 surveyed)
basis.measured: Past-year status: still dependent 25.0%, some symptoms left 27.3%, risky drinking without symptoms 11.8%, low-risk drinking 17.7%, not drinking 18.2%. Plus: ever treated or not.

stats.caveat: It does not show that the untreated did as well as the treated. 'Not hooked' includes people with some symptoms left or risky drinking.

ref.cite: Dawson DA, Grant BF, Stinson FS, Chou PS, Huang B, Ruan WJ (2005). Recovery from DSM-IV alcohol dependence: United States, 2001-2002. Addiction.
ref.quote: Of people classified with PPY alcohol dependence, 25.0% were still classified as dependent in the past year … Only 25.5% of people with PPY dependence ever received treatment.

stats.line: People who got help (treatment or AA) in their first year were more often free of problem drinking 3 years later: 62% against 43%.
stats.mirror: You think getting help is weak and want to do it alone.

basis.design: cohort followed 16 years
basis.who: adults with a drinking problem, never treated before, who had just contacted a referral centre or detox; mean age 33.5, half men
basis.n: 362 who got help vs 99 who didn't (461 in all)
basis.measured: Free at 3 years: no drinking or moderate drinking in each of the past 6 months, no drinking problems, no intoxication in the past month. Of those free at 3 years, 60.5% without help and 42.9% with help slid back by year 16.

stats.caveat: Not a trial: people chose whether to get help, so they may differ in other ways. Slipping back was common in both groups.

ref.cite: Moos RH, Moos BS (2006). Rates and predictors of relapse after natural and treated remission from alcohol use disorders. Addiction.
ref.quote: By the 3-year follow-up, 62.4% of individuals in the helped group were remitted, compared with only 43.4% of individuals in the no help group

stats.line: After one month off alcohol, regular drinkers' insulin resistance fell about 26%, their blood pressure about 6%, and their weight 1.5%.
stats.mirror: You drink every week and wonder what a month off would do.

basis.design: prospective observational study (people chose to stop or not)
basis.who: healthy adults drinking more than 64 g a week (men), mean age about 45; not alcohol dependent
basis.n: 94 people who stopped (47 who kept drinking, for comparison)
basis.when: Published 2018; the paper doesn't give the study dates
basis.measured: Blood tests, blood pressure and weight before and after one month. The group that kept drinking showed no significant change.

stats.caveat: Small study, not a trial. Volunteers were not dependent, and nothing shows how long the gains last if drinking resumes.

ref.cite: Mehta G, Macdonald S, Cronberg A, et al. (2018). Short-term abstinence from alcohol and changes in cardiovascular risk factors, liver function tests and cancer-related growth factors: a prospective observational study. BMJ Open.
ref.quote: HOMA score (-25.9%, IQR -48.6% to +0.3%), systolic BP (-6.6%, IQR -11.8% to 0.0%) … weight (-1.5%, IQR -2.9% to -0.4%)

stats.line: After beating a drinking or drug problem, quality of life, happiness and self-esteem climb steeply for about 6 years, then keep rising more slowly.
stats.mirror: You wonder if sober life ever gets better than this.

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot
basis.who: adults who said they used to have an alcohol or drug problem but no longer do
basis.n: 2,002 adults (of 39,809 screened)
basis.measured: Quality of life, happiness, self-esteem, recovery resources and distress, compared across people 0 to 40 years past their problem.

stats.caveat: Happiness and self-esteem dipped in the first year before rising. Different people at different stages, not the same people followed.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG (2018). Beyond abstinence: changes in indices of quality of life with time in recovery in a nationally representative sample of U.S. adults. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
ref.quote: In general, in the 40-year horizon there were initially steep increases in indices of well-being (and steep drops in distress), during the first 6 years, followed by shallower increases.

stats.line: Half of Americans who got hooked on alcohol were free of every sign of it within about 14 years. By the time they were asked, 2,008 of 4,781 already were.
stats.mirror: You've been drinking hard for ten years and think it's too late.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; ages recalled and modelled over a lifetime
basis.who: adults who had ever been dependent on alcohol
basis.n: 4,781 adults who had ever been hooked (of 43,093 surveyed); 2,008 of them had got free
basis.measured: The age when the signs of being hooked first appeared, and the age when they finally stopped and never came back, as people recalled it. Getting free here means no signs of being hooked any more; it does not have to mean never using. Cigarettes took 26 years, weed 6, cocaine 5.

stats.caveat: The study projects that about 9 in 10 get free at some point in life; that is a model, not a head count. Men got free more slowly than women.

ref.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, Pines A, Wang S, Grant BF, Blanco C (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from the National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. Addiction.
ref.quote: Half of the cases of nicotine, alcohol, cannabis and cocaine dependence remitted approximately 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after dependence onset, respectively.

stats.line: Americans who beat a drinking problem were about 38, on average, when it ended. People who beat a weed problem were about 29.
stats.mirror: You're in your thirties and think people your age don't change.

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot
basis.who: adults who said they used to have a problem with alcohol or drugs but no longer do, and named alcohol as the main one
basis.n: About 1,013 people whose main problem was alcohol (a weighted count, of 2,002)
basis.measured: Age when the problem ended, as people remembered it. On average they had used alcohol for about 18 years before that.

stats.caveat: An average: many got free much younger or older. It counts only people who got free, not those still drinking.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG (2018). Is recovery from cannabis use problems different from alcohol and other drugs? Results from a national probability-based sample of the United States adult population. International Journal of Drug Policy.
ref.quote: resolved their problem significantly earlier (CAN M = 28.87, ALC M = 37.86, OTH M = 33.06, p < 0.01)

stats.line: In the 3 years after becoming a parent for the first time, people hooked on alcohol were about twice as likely to get free by stopping drinking.
stats.mirror: You're about to be a dad and want to stop drinking.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews; life events dated from memory
basis.who: adults whose alcohol dependence began before the past year
basis.n: 4,422 adults who had been hooked (of 43,093 surveyed)
basis.measured: How the chance of getting free changed in the years after leaving school, starting full-time work, marrying, splitting up and becoming a parent. A first marriage raised the chance of getting free while still drinking lightly (×1.37); so did a first marriage ending (×1.76).

stats.caveat: A link, not proof: people ready to change may also be the ones starting families. Men and women together. People still hooked 3+ years after marrying or leaving school got free less often afterwards.

ref.cite: Dawson DA, Grant BF, Stinson FS, Chou PS (2006). Maturing out of alcohol dependence: the impact of transitional life events. Journal of Studies on Alcohol.
ref.quote: The likelihood of AR was more than doubled in the 3 years after first becoming a parent (HRR = 2.22)

stats.line: Of Americans who beat a drinking problem, 56% had used some help along the way: meetings like AA, treatment, or medication. The rest never used any.
stats.mirror: You think nobody quits drinking without AA.

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey), one snapshot
basis.who: adults who said they used to have a problem with alcohol or drugs but no longer do, and named alcohol as the main one
basis.n: About 1,013 people whose main problem was alcohol (a weighted count, of 2,002)
basis.measured: Ever used, at any point: mutual-help groups (such as AA), treatment, medication or recovery services. Across all substances 54% used help; mutual-help groups were the most common (45%). AA alone: 35%.

stats.caveat: Help could be one meeting years ago or years of treatment. It doesn't show which route worked better; people with worse problems used help more.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Bergman B, Hoeppner BB, Vilsaint C, White WL (2017). Prevalence and pathways of recovery from drug and alcohol problems in the United States population: implications for practice, research, and policy. Drug and Alcohol Dependence.
ref.quote: Factors associated with choosing assisted (54%) vs. unassisted problem resolution. … Alcohol 55.9

stats.line: Of Americans who beat a drinking or drug problem after at least one serious try, half needed 3 tries or fewer. A few needed many more.
stats.mirror: You've tried to stop before and think you've failed for good.

basis.design: national survey (National Recovery Survey)
basis.who: adults who said they used to have an alcohol or drug problem but no longer do, and had made at least one serious try
basis.n: 1,742 people (of 2,002 in the study; about 1 in 8 never made a serious try)
basis.measured: Number of serious tries before the problem was resolved, as people remembered it. Counting everyone, including those who never made a serious try, the middle figure was 2.

stats.caveat: Counts only people who succeeded, from memory. The average was about 6 because a few people needed dozens of tries.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Greene MC, Bergman BG, White WL, Hoeppner BB (2019). How many recovery attempts does it take to successfully resolve an alcohol or drug problem? Estimates and correlates from a national study of recovering U.S. adults. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
ref.quote: among participants reporting at least 1 serious recovery attempt (n = 1,742), the mean and median number of recovery attempts were slightly higher—6.14 (SD = 14.20) and 3

stats.line: Of Americans once hooked on alcohol, as many now drank lightly with no problems (18%) as didn't drink at all (18%).
stats.mirror: You wonder if quitting has to mean never drinking again.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), face-to-face interviews
basis.who: adults whose alcohol dependence began before the past year
basis.n: 4,422 adults who had been hooked before the past year (of 43,093 surveyed)
basis.measured: Past-year drinking, from interviews. Light drinking: no signs of a problem and below risky amounts. Another 12% had no signs but drank risky amounts, a pattern the authors say puts people at risk of sliding back; 25% were still hooked.

stats.caveat: A snapshot, not a follow-up. Light drinkers had usually been less badly hooked. Three years later, problems came back more often for light drinkers than for non-drinkers.

ref.cite: Dawson DA, Grant BF, Stinson FS, Chou PS, Huang B, Ruan WJ (2005). Recovery from DSM-IV alcohol dependence: United States, 2001-2002. Addiction.
ref.quote: 11.8% were asymptomatic risk drinkers who demonstrated a pattern of drinking that put them at risk of relapse; 17.7% were low-risk drinkers; and 18.2% were abstainers.

stats.line: Of Americans who had got free of alcohol, problems came back within 3 years for 27% of those who kept drinking lightly, and 7% of those who stopped. Full addiction came back for 4% and 3%.
stats.mirror: You've been off it a while and think you could drink normally now.

basis.design: national survey (NESARC), the same people interviewed twice, 3 years apart
basis.who: adults fully free of alcohol dependence at the first interview
basis.n: 1,772 people re-interviewed (of 2,109 who were free at the first interview); the study summary doesn't say how many were in each group
basis.measured: Any sign of a drinking problem coming back, and full dependence coming back, by the second interview: light drinkers against non-drinkers. Of those who had no signs but drank risky amounts, 51% had problems back.

stats.caveat: Not a trial: people chose whether to drink. Weighing other differences, the odds of problems coming back were 5.8 times as high for light drinkers. For young adults the gap wasn't clear: they slid back most either way.

ref.cite: Dawson DA, Goldstein RB, Grant BF (2007). Rates and correlates of relapse among individuals in remission from DSM-IV alcohol dependence: a 3-year follow-up. Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research.
ref.quote: By Wave 2, 51.0% of the Wave 1 asymptomatic risk drinkers had experienced the recurrence of AUD symptoms, compared with 27.2% of low-risk drinkers and 7.3% of abstainers.

stats.line: Therapy built to get people going to AA kept about 1.2 times as many fully off drink for a year as other proven talking therapies.
stats.mirror: You think AA is the last thing that would work for you.

basis.design: Cochrane review; this figure pools 2 randomised trials
basis.who: adults with a drinking problem who weren't forced into treatment
basis.n: 1,936 people in 2 trials (of 27 studies with 10,565 people in the review)
basis.where: The review summary doesn't name the countries of these 2 trials
basis.measured: Not drinking at all, without a break, for 12 months: 12-step facilitation from a manual (therapy that steers people into AA) against other set therapies such as CBT. The gap held at 24 and 36 months.

stats.caveat: It tests a therapist steering you into AA, not AA alone. On how much people drank when they did drink, AA-based help did about as well as other therapy, not better.

ref.cite: Kelly JF, Humphreys K, Ferri M (2020). Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews.
ref.quote: AA/TSF improves rates of continuous abstinence at 12 months (risk ratio (RR) 1.21, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.03 to 1.42; 2 studies, 1936 participants; high-certainty evidence)

stats.line: For every 12 people who take the medicine acamprosate, one more stays off drink than would without it.
stats.mirror: You didn't know there are pills that help people stop drinking.

basis.design: meta-analysis of 122 randomised trials and 1 cohort study
basis.who: adults with alcohol use disorder treated as outpatients
basis.n: 4,847 people in 16 trials (of 122 trials in the review)
basis.where: Mostly Europe (16 of 22 placebo trials of acamprosate)
basis.measured: Return to any drinking during trials of at least 12 weeks, acamprosate against placebo. Naltrexone: one in 20 for any drinking, one in 12 for heavy drinking.

stats.caveat: One in 12 is a modest effect: it helps some people, not everyone. It needs a prescription.

ref.cite: Jonas DE, Amick HR, Feltner C, et al. (2014). Pharmacotherapy for adults with alcohol use disorders in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA.
ref.quote: The NNT to prevent return to any drinking for acamprosate was 12 (95% CI, 8 to 26; risk difference [RD], -0.09; 95% CI, -0.14 to -0.04)

rejected.claim: Page number '90% of US heavy drinkers don't meet the criteria for dependence' (existing).
rejected.why: Number checks out, word does not. The study counts 'excessive drinkers': binge, heavy, under-21 or pregnant drinking; about 90% of them binge. Correct: '90% of US adults who drink excessively, mostly binge drinkers'.

rejected.claim: Page number '2.6 million deaths worldwide in 2019' (existing).
rejected.why: Dropped on the owner's instruction (no population death tolls).

rejected.claim: The top 10% of US drinkers average about 74 drinks a week.
rejected.why: Only found in Philip Cook's book 'Paying the Tab' (2007) as retold by newspapers and blogs; figures were scaled up 1.97x to match sales. No primary or official source fetched.

rejected.claim: Dry January: '71% slept better' and similar benefit percentages.
rejected.why: Those figures come from the charity Alcohol Change UK. The peer-reviewed study (de Visser 2020, PMID 32391879) reports benefits but gives no numbers in its abstract.

rejected.claim: Heavy drinking raises divorce risk: hazard ratio 1.51 when only the husband drinks heavily (19,977 Norwegian couples, 15 years).
rejected.why: Verified (Torvik 2013, PMID 23384147) but cut to stay at 14 stats; the abstract does not define 'heavy drinking'.

rejected.claim: 36% of US men meet alcohol use disorder criteria at some point in life; only 19.8% of people with it are ever treated (NESARC-III, 36,309 adults, 2012-13).
rejected.why: Verified (Grant 2015, PMID 26039070) but cut to stay at 14; overlaps the NSDUH and Dawson stats.

rejected.claim: About 46% of Americans who resolved an alcohol or drug problem did it without any help.
rejected.why: Not stated as such: the paper gives 53.9% who used help, for alcohol and drugs together (Kelly 2017, PMID 29055821). Not used.

rejected.claim: A drinking problem comes with about twice the odds of major depression; alcohol seems to drive the depression more than the other way round (Boden 2011, pooled AORs 2.00–2.09).
rejected.why: Dropped: the publisher page returned 403 and the abstract gives no number of studies or people, so the figure cannot show what it is based on.

rejected.claim: Project MATCH (1,726 people) and UKATT (742 people): very different alcohol therapies gave about the same results.
rejected.why: Verified (PMIDs 8979210, 16150764), but neither summary gives one plain number to show; the AA review stat covers 'which therapy'.

rejected.claim: Only about 1.6% of Americans with a drinking problem get medicine for it (Han 2021, NSDUH 2019).
rejected.why: The research letter's text could not be read (the PMC record has no body text), so the figure is unchecked.

rejected.claim: 23% of Americans who beat a drinking problem define recovery as moderate drinking (Kelly 2018 table).
rejected.why: Table-only figure about how people define recovery, not what they do; Dawson 2005 (18% light drinkers) used instead.
